prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory and showing how reallocation across firms shapes trade patterns and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1 (B048, Melitz and Helpman, with B001 and B037 as alternatives). The exchange sharpened my reasons and the citation wording. I judge candidates by three criteria: what was established, how well it has survived testing, and whether the credit divides cleanly. On the first, the selection and reallocation mechanism changed the unit of analysis in trade from the sector to the firm. It identified a distinct channel for gains from trade and made firm-level data the standard test bed. On the second, the qualitative predictions (exporter premia, selection into exporting, within-industry reallocation after liberalisation) have been checked in many countries over more than twenty years. The disputes concern magnitudes and functional form, not the mechanism. On the third, Melitz (2003) is the originating model and Helpman's exporting-versus-FDI work with Melitz and Yeaple is tightly linked to it. The chair's summary shows seven explicit B048 preferences. I do not treat that as evidence of merit. What I find informative is that the attribution reasoning is independent across members and converges. I have also tightened the citation to the selection and reallocation mechanism, so that it does not claim priority over the empirical firm-level facts. As someone who works on institutional measurement, I hold B001 to the standard I apply elsewhere: its lasting contribution is the data and facts, while the identified causal content is the contested part. A prize credits a discovery, and the strongest version of B001's discovery is the part least settled.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is priority. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (and Yeaple) developed closely parallel firm-level facts and models, and they are not on this ballot entry. A Melitz-Helpman citation could be read as under-crediting the empirical foundations, even if it is worded around the theoretical mechanism. The welfare magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, and some empirical support for the predictions is only partial. Helpman also appears in another package (B026), which could complicate his framing. Excluding Redding is a judgement call. I treat his quantitative and spatial work as a later wave that builds on the framework. If the Committee judged the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question to be material and uncorrectable by wording, the case for B048 would weaken and B001 would come closer, although I would still weigh B001's Vishny exclusion and the contested causal core. Finally, trade was recognised in 2008. I treat that as a timing and field-balance consideration, not evidence about this work.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B001 and calls the gap with B048 small. He would word the citation around measurable legal institutions and the established link between investor protection and financial outcomes, not the strong legal-origins causal reading. He argues that creating a new field is more decisive than refining an established one.
responses.response: I accept that a citation limited to measurement and established regularities is more defensible than one endorsing legal origin as a cause, and that it answers part of my objection. Two difficulties remain. First, once the causal reading is set aside, what is credited is mainly data and a research design. That is an important contribution, but it is a thinner discovery than a mechanism that generated and passed out-of-sample tests. Second, a prize for that body of work excludes Vishny, who co-authored the founding papers, and the cap makes this unavoidable. I do not agree that B048 only refines an established field. Melitz (2003) changed what a trade model must explain and opened a new empirical agenda. I regard the gap as small, but it favours B048 on robustness and on cleaner attribution.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B001 with moderate confidence. He concedes it would not compete on identification credibility alone, and he rests his case on the field-creating contribution and the long period of testing. He argues that the critiques are themselves evidence of maturity.
responses.response: I value his candour that B001's case does not rest on identification strength. That is where we differ. I agree that critique is a sign of maturity. But maturity means the central claims have been tested, and the question is how they fared. For B048, the qualitative core held up under testing. For B001, the central causal claim and the coding of the indices were qualified. A prize could still recognise the field-creating contribution. If the Committee decides to do so, I would want the citation worded around the data and facts, as he suggests. Head to head under that wording, I would still prefer B048, because its credit divides cleanly into two names and the other requires leaving out a co-author of the core papers.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B001 and ranked B048 sixth. He argues that the critiques qualify the mechanism more than the discovery, and that the cross-country regularities and the research agenda survive even if the legal-origin story is only partly causal. He also says he cannot assess conduct controversies from the supplied evidence.
responses.response: I agree with his refusal to count conduct controversies as merit. They are not documented in the permitted materials and should stay outside our evaluation. I accept that the cross-country regularities would survive a partial causal story. But I read the critiques differently. In my own work on institutional measurement, a proxy for deeper historical factors is a problem for identification, and that is the question a prize citation has to answer. On B048, his earlier point that empirical support is only partial deserves care. I read it as applying to magnitudes and functional form, and much less to the qualitative selection predictions. So I would treat his reservation as a reason to word the citation around the mechanism, not as a reason to rank B048 below B001.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B037 (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler) and would accept a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version if Gertler's credit is judged too entangled with B040. He distinguishes the 2022 prize on banks and crises from the collateral amplification mechanism, and he lists B048 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I accept his distinction. Kiyotaki and Moore is a clean, mature and widely reused mechanism, and I keep B037 as an alternative for that reason. I do not treat the 2022 prize as disqualifying. It narrows the marginal novelty. The unclear point is Gertler. His credit is split with B040 and with the Bernanke accelerator lineage, and Gilchrist is excluded, so a three-name version is harder to defend than the two-name core. The identification of collateral channels is also less settled than the theory's influence. I read this as meaning B037 would be strongest as a two-name, mechanism-focused citation. Even then, B048 has the broader support among members for its attribution and for how well its predictions have tested. That is why I still place B037 behind B048, as an alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B048 and calls the parallel Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum work the real vulnerability, because it concerns priority on the empirical foundations, not only a later extension. She would draft the citation around the selection mechanism and the gains-from-trade framework.
responses.response: I agree with her diagnosis and with the remedy, and it answers the chair's first question for B048 supporters. A citation limited to the selection and reallocation mechanism is sufficient for my preference. It credits what Melitz and Helpman carried, and it does not claim the firm-level facts. I would add one limit. Wording cannot fully remove the priority question, and if the Committee judged it material, I would say so openly and not treat it as resolved. That would reduce the margin between B048 and B001 for me, but it would not reverse the order, since B001 has its own unresolved attribution problem in Vishny.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee judges the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question material, and if so whether mechanism-focused wording is a sufficient remedy.
How the Committee separates thematic overlap with recent prizes (2022 to 2025) and the 2008 trade prize, which I treat as timing or field-balance considerations, from scientific merit.
How the dependence of welfare-gain magnitudes on functional form (for example Pareto productivity) bears on the claim of a robust discovery, as opposed to a robust qualitative mechanism.
Whether Helpman's appearance on B026 affects his claim on B048. I read it as a reason to define the citation tightly, not to discount his claim.

Whether B001's contribution is judged to be the data and research design, as its supporters argue, or the legal-origins causal reading, as its critics argue. This determines how close B001 is to B048 for me. All assessments rely on my own knowledge of the literature, which I have not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No documented connection to Melitz or Helpman, the credited names in my preferred part. For completeness, I co-authored with Torsten Persson (with Bo Rothstein) on corruption as a collective-action problem. Persson is credited on B049, which I do not propose and do not list as an alternative. I work at Stockholm University, where committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart are colleagues in a different department. As a political scientist I work on institutions and their measurement, which is close to the themes of B001 and B049. I disclose possible proximity bias and have applied the same criteria to every field. I gave the 2024 presentation speech, but speeches for the Academy may reflect collective drafting and do not establish my preferences. These are disclosed, not adjudicated.
